{{Short description|Theorem in representation theory}}
In [[representation theory]], a branch of mathematics, the '''theorem of the highest weight''' classifies the [[Lie algebra representation#Classifying finite-dimensional representations of Lie algebras|irreducible representations]] of a complex [[semisimple Lie algebra]] <math>\mathfrak g</math>.<ref>{{harvnb|Dixmier|1996|loc=Theorem 7.2.6.}}</ref><ref name="9.4 and 9.5">{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Theorems 9.4 and 9.5</ref> There is a closely related theorem classifying the [[Compact group#Representation theory of a connected compact Lie group|irreducible representations]] of a connected compact [[Lie group]] <math>K</math>.<ref name="12.6">{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Theorem 12.6</ref> The theorem states that there is a bijection
:<math>\lambda \mapsto [V^\lambda]</math>
from the set of "dominant integral elements" to the set of equivalence classes of irreducible representations of <math>\mathfrak g</math> or <math>K</math>. The difference between the two results is in the precise notion of "integral" in the definition of a dominant integral element. If <math>K</math> is simply connected, this distinction disappears.

The theorem was originally proved by [[Élie Cartan]] in his 1913 paper.<ref>{{Cite journal|url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/3647845|jstor=3647845|last1=Knapp|first1=A. W.|title=Reviewed work: Matrix Groups: An Introduction to Lie Group Theory, Andrew Baker; Lie Groups: An Introduction through Linear Groups, Wulf Rossmann|journal=The American Mathematical Monthly|year=2003|volume=110|issue=5|pages=446–455|doi=10.2307/3647845|url-access=subscription}}</ref> The version of the theorem for a compact Lie group is due to [[Hermann Weyl]]. The theorem is one of the key pieces of [[representation theory of semisimple Lie algebras]].

== Statement ==
=== Lie algebra case ===
{{see also|Weight (representation theory)#Weights in the representation theory of semisimple Lie algebras}}
Let <math>\mathfrak{g}</math> be a finite-dimensional semisimple [[complex Lie algebra]] with [[Cartan subalgebra]] <math>\mathfrak{h}</math>. Let <math>R</math> be the associated [[root system]]. We then say that an element <math>\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*</math> is '''integral'''<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Section 8.7</ref> if 
:<math>2\frac{\langle\lambda,\alpha\rangle}{\langle\alpha,\alpha\rangle}</math>
is an integer for each root <math>\alpha</math>. Next, we choose a set <math>R^+</math> of positive roots and we say that an element <math>\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*</math> is '''dominant''' if <math>\langle\lambda,\alpha\rangle\geq 0</math> for all <math>\alpha\in R^+</math>. An element <math>\lambda\in\mathfrak h^*</math> is '''dominant integral''' if it is both dominant and integral. Finally, if <math>\lambda</math> and <math>\mu</math> are in <math>\mathfrak h^*</math>, we say that <math>\lambda</math> is '''higher'''<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Section 8.8</ref> than <math>\mu</math> if <math>\lambda-\mu</math> is expressible as a linear combination of positive roots with non-negative real coefficients.

A [[Weight (representation theory)#Weights in the representation theory of semisimple Lie algebras|weight]] <math>\lambda</math> of a representation <math>V</math> of <math>\mathfrak g</math> is then called a '''highest weight''' if <math>\lambda</math> is higher than every other weight <math>\mu</math> of <math>V</math>.

The theorem of the highest weight then states:<ref name="9.4 and 9.5" />
*If <math>V</math> is a finite-dimensional irreducible representation of <math>\mathfrak{g}</math>, then <math>V</math> has a unique highest weight, and this highest weight is dominant integral.
*If two finite-dimensional irreducible representations have the same highest weight, they are isomorphic.
*For each dominant integral element <math>\lambda</math>, there exists a finite-dimensional irreducible representation with highest weight <math>\lambda</math>.

The most difficult part is the last one; the construction of a finite-dimensional irreducible representation with a prescribed highest weight.

=== The compact group case ===
{{see also|Compact group#Representation theory of a connected compact Lie group}}
Let <math>K</math> be a connected [[compact group|compact Lie group]] with Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak k</math> and let <math>\mathfrak g:=\mathfrak k+i\mathfrak k</math> be the complexification of <math>\mathfrak k</math>. Let <math>T</math> be a [[maximal torus]] in <math>K</math> with Lie algebra <math>\mathfrak t</math>. Then <math>\mathfrak h:=\mathfrak t+i\mathfrak t</math> is a Cartan subalgebra of <math>\mathfrak g</math>, and we may form the associated root system <math>R</math>. The theory then proceeds in much the same way as in the Lie algebra case, with one crucial difference: the notion of integrality is different. Specifically, we say that an element <math>\lambda\in\mathfrak h</math> is ''' analytically integral'''<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Definition 12.4</ref> if 
:<math>\langle\lambda,H\rangle</math>
is an integer whenever
:<math>e^{2\pi H}=I</math>
where <math>I</math> is the identity element of <math>K</math>. Every analytically integral element is integral in the Lie algebra sense,<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Proposition 12.7</ref> but there may be integral elements in the Lie algebra sense that are not analytically integral. This distinction reflects the fact that if <math>K</math> is not simply connected, there may be representations of <math>\mathfrak g</math> that do not come from representations of <math>K</math>. On the other hand, if <math>K</math> is simply connected, the notions of "integral" and "analytically integral" coincide.<ref name="12.6" />

The theorem of the highest weight for representations of <math>K</math><ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Corollary 13.20</ref> is then the same as in the Lie algebra case, except that "integral" is replaced by "analytically integral."

== Proofs ==
There are at least four proofs:
*Hermann Weyl's original proof from the compact group point of view,<ref>{{harvnb|Hall|2015}} Chapter 12</ref> based on the [[Weyl character formula]] and the [[Peter–Weyl theorem]]. 
*The theory of [[Verma module]]s contains the highest weight theorem. This is the approach taken in many standard textbooks (e.g., Humphreys and Part II of Hall).
*The [[Borel–Weil–Bott theorem]] constructs an irreducible representation as the space of global sections of an ample line bundle; the highest weight theorem results as a consequence. (The approach uses a fair bit of algebraic geometry but yields a very quick proof.)
*The [[invariant theory|invariant theoretic]] approach: one constructs irreducible representations as subrepresentations of a tensor power of the standard representations. This approach is essentially due to H. Weyl and works quite well for classical groups.
